title: Integration and Regional Aspirations

cards.h: A country many said would break up
cards.b:
In 1947, India had two problems at once: a Partition that killed lakhs and displaced millions, and over 560 princely states that could join India, join Pakistan or stand alone. Many outsiders expected the country to fragment. Selig Harrison wrote India: The Most Dangerous Decades (1960) predicting exactly that.

It did not happen. India today has 28 states and 8 Union Territories (2020 count after Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu merged).

Why did a diverse country hold together while still facing repeated demands for new states, autonomy or independence? The answer lies in how it integrated the princely states, drew its internal borders, and made room for regional identity in the Constitution.

This lesson asks you to explain both the successes and the failures. Examiners like the question "How has Indian federalism accommodated regional aspirations?"

The British paramountcy lapsed on 15 August 1947. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, with his secretary V.P. Menon, led the States Department. Their tools were:

  • The Instrument of Accession: states handed over defence, external affairs and communications.
  • Persuasion and the fear of popular movements within the states.
  • Later merger and integration: small states merged into provinces or formed unions (such as PEPSU or Rajasthan); larger ones such as Mysore and Hyderabad became Part B states under the 1950 Constitution.
  • Generous privy purses in return, which Indira Gandhi's government ended through the 26th Amendment (1971) after the Supreme Court had struck down her derecognition order in 1970.

Three cases were hard. Junagadh: its Nawab acceded to Pakistan; a plebiscite in February 1948 favoured India. Hyderabad: the Nizam refused, then the army moved in during Operation Polo (September 1948). Jammu and Kashmir: Maharaja Hari Singh signed accession on 26 October 1947 during the tribal invasion.

See V.P. Menon's The Story of the Integration of the Indian States (1956).

• Pondicherry: French rule ended in 1954; added to the Constitution by the 14th Amendment (1962).
  • Goa, Daman and Diu: liberated from Portugal in December 1961 (Operation Vijay). Goa became a state in 1987.
  • Sikkim: a protectorate; merged in 1975 through the 36th Amendment as a full state.
  • Northeast: hill peoples were never fully ruled by princes. The Sixth Schedule covered them from the start.

The Constitution lets Parliament admit or form new states by Articles 2 and 3. In Article 3 the state legislature is only consulted; Parliament decides. This is why Telangana (2014) and J&K (2019) could be created without state consent.

cards.h: Linguistic reorganisation: from fear to acceptance
cards.b:
The Congress had promised linguistic provinces since the 1920s. After Partition, leaders feared a second break-up. The Dar Commission (1948) and the JVP Committee (Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya, 1949) advised against language as the basis.

The mood changed after Potti Sriramulu died on 15 December 1952 after a fast for a Telugu state. Andhra was formed on 1 October 1953.

The States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru, report 1955) accepted language as a main basis, but stressed unity and the needs of finance and defence. The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 made 14 states and 6 Union Territories.

• 1960: Bombay state split into Maharashtra and Gujarat after the Samyukta Maharashtra movement.
  • 1963: Nagaland.
  • 1966: Punjab split into Punjab and Haryana (Punjabi-speaking state demand by Akali Dal; Shah Commission). Himachal got statehood in 1971.
  • 1972: Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura became states (North-Eastern Areas Reorganisation Act).
  • 1987: Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa.
  • 2000: Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand, carved out peacefully on grounds of governance and tribal identity, not language.
  • 2014: Telangana, the 29th state, under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014.
  • 2019: The J&K Reorganisation Act turned the state into two Union Territories: J&K (with a legislature) and Ladakh (without).

Today, language is no longer treated as dangerous. Many scholars say that giving language its place strengthened the Union.

cards.h: Thinkers on India's diversity and unity
cards.b:
Selig Harrison, The Most Dangerous Decades (1960)

Predicted that language and regional loyalties would break India apart. History proved him wrong.

Paul Brass, Language, Religion and Politics in North India (1974); The Politics of India since Independence (1990)

Ethnic and linguistic groups are not natural. Elites build identity and use it to win resources. This is the instrumentalist view.

Myron Weiner, Sons of the Soil (1978)

Migration and job competition produce nativist movements, as seen in Assam and Maharashtra.

Stepan, Linz and Yadav, Crafting State-Nations (2011)

India is a state-nation, not a nation-state: it respects many cultural identities and builds loyalty to the state through democracy, federal accommodation and multiple languages. Unlike France, it did not force a single identity.

Atul Kohli, Democracy and Discontent (1990)

Argued India faced a "crisis of governability" as institutions weakened and demands rose.

Not every regional demand is the same. Sort them into four types:

  1. Secession or sovereignty: Naga National Council under A.Z. Phizo; Mizo National Front under Laldenga (1966); Khalistan militancy; Kashmir insurgency (from 1989). The DMK's early call for a Dravida Nadu led to the 16th Amendment (1963), which allows restrictions on speech and requires an oath to uphold sovereignty and integrity.
  2. Statehood within the Union: Telangana, Vidarbha, Gorkhaland, Bodoland, Harit Pradesh.
  3. Autonomy and language rights: anti-Hindi agitation in Tamil Nadu (1965), Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973), West Bengal and Tamil Nadu demands for more power.
  4. Nativism or "sons of the soil": Assam Movement (1979-85), Shiv Sena in its early phase.

India used accords with the main insurgent groups to bring them into democratic politics: the Punjab Accord (Rajiv-Longowal, July 1985), Assam Accord (August 1985), Mizo Accord (1986, Mizoram statehood in 1987).

• Fifth and Sixth Schedules (Article 244) for tribal areas. The Sixth Schedule gives Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
  • Special provisions, Articles 371 to 371J: Nagaland (371A, 13th Amendment 1962: Parliament cannot override Naga customary law without Assembly consent), Assam (371B), Manipur (371C), Andhra and Telangana (371D, 371E), Sikkim (371F), Mizoram (371G), Arunachal (371H), Goa (371I) and Hyderabad-Karnataka (371J, 98th Amendment 2012).
  • Eighth Schedule: 22 languages. The 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali.
  • Article 370 gave J&K special status until it was revoked on 5 August 2019.
  • Autonomous councils by accord: Bodoland Territorial Council (2003, revised accord January 2020), Gorkhaland Territorial Administration (2012).

This is asymmetric federalism: different units hold different powers.

The success view (Stepan, Linz, Yadav; Ashutosh Varshney in Battles Half Won, 2013): democracy, flexible borders and language recognition tied peripheries to the centre. Most separatist movements ended in accords, not partition.

The critical view:

  • Accords are not always carried out. Naga talks (Framework Agreement 2015) remain unresolved.
  • AFSPA and long militarisation in the Northeast and J&K have hurt rights and trust.
  • New states create new minorities within, such as Gorkhas in Bengal or Kuki-Zo groups in Manipur.
  • Unequal development fuels demands (Vidarbha, Bundelkhand).
  • The Centre sometimes ignores regional voices: the 2019 J&K change was made without a state assembly.

A balanced answer says India has been good at accommodation but weaker at resolution.

• J&K and Ladakh: the Constitution Bench in In re: Article 370 (11 December 2023, CJI Chandrachud) upheld the revocation, accepted that J&K had no internal sovereignty, and asked for statehood to be restored "at the earliest". Assembly elections were held in 2024 and Omar Abdullah became Chief Minister. Statehood had not been restored in the reports I could find. Ladakh saw protests in September 2025 for statehood and Sixth Schedule status.
  • Manipur: Meitei-Kuki violence began in May 2023. President's Rule ran from 13 February 2025 and was revoked on 4 February 2026, when Yumnam Khemchand Singh took office as Chief Minister.
  • Language: disputes over the three-language policy in NEP 2020 and over Hindi in states like Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra.
  • Delimitation: southern states fear that a post-Census 2027 seat adjustment could reduce their weight in Lok Sabha.
  • Bodo and Karbi accords (2020, 2021) show the accord route continues.

Structure: start from 1947 fears (Harrison); princely states; Dar/JVP to SRC and the 1956 Act; later states; types of demands; constitutional accommodation (Schedules, Article 371, accords); Stepan-Linz-Yadav's state-nation; critique (AFSPA, Manipur, Ladakh); a balanced conclusion.

quiz.q: Who headed the States Department that integrated princely states?
quiz.w: Patel, with V.P. Menon as secretary.

quiz.q: Which commission (1955) recommended language as the main basis of reorganisation?
quiz.w: The States Reorganisation Commission under Fazl Ali.

quiz.q: Whose death after a fast in 1952 hastened the formation of Andhra?
quiz.w: Potti Sriramulu, 15 December 1952; Andhra formed on 1 October 1953.

quiz.q: Which amendment ended the privy purses?
Sikkim became a full state through which amendment?

quiz.w: Nagaland's customary law and land (13th Amendment, 1962).
